266: The 2008 Stockholm Water Prize was awarded to Professor Tony Allan, who proposed the concept of "virtual water."
267: "Virtual water" refers to the amount of water needed in producing and selling food or consumer goods.
268: The concept points out that people need water not only for drinking and showering, but also consume large amounts of water when they consume other products.
269: For example, a cup of coffee uses 140 liters of water during growing, production, packaging and transport—equivalent to the average daily water use of a British person for drinking and household life.
270: The concept of "virtual water" further explains the trading model of "virtual water," which has had a major impact on global trade policy and water resource use.
271: The theory points out that agriculture in humid regions mostly uses cheap natural rainfall rather than costly irrigation systems, and can therefore greatly reduce agricultural production costs.
272: These regions can "export" water resources to hotter, drier countries through crops.
273: And countries with dry climates can "import" water-intensive crops, relieving the pressure of insufficient domestic water.
274: Although only agricultural products are visible in the trade, it actually includes an exchange of water resources.
275: For example, in Egypt, more and more traditional foods are made from imported grain rather than from wheat irrigated by the Nile.
276: If Egypt insisted on growing all its grain itself, it would soon face a water shortage.
277: A report from World Water Week also used this concept, pointing out that the current global food crisis lies in excessive waste rather than insufficient production.
278: Because every step of a portion of food—production, processing, transport, storage, sale and cooking—consumes water, if consumers throw away food they've bought, it also means wasting the water used in growing, transporting and storing it.
